method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0' (MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018), 21 claims; LICENCE: Not stated on the criteria pages (NBA's site-wide CC BY 4.0 at blood.gov.au/copyright not confirmed for criteria.blood.gov.au) (read at https://www.blood.gov.au/copyright (read 2026-09-23); criteria pages carry no licence notice). S2: QUOTED from German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes' (published 26 December 2023), 12 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC10752078). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every edition 1.0 claim (S1, National Blood Authority IVIg criteria) unchanged and adds S2, the German Neurological Society guideline for myasthenic syndromes (2023, CC BY), which S1's own Unresolved table named as the candidate. S1 is Australian, so the most current open international society guideline was added. The Association of British Neurologists 2025 update (Pract Neurol) was not used: it needs a login. The MGFA international consensus 2020 update predates the C5 and FcRn inhibitors and is CC BY-NC-ND.

claims.claim: **MG is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction** with antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) or to MuSK; a minority of patients are seronegative.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Suspect it in fatigable, fluctuating weakness** of the eyelids, eye movements, bulbar, limb and breathing muscles: ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia and proximal weakness. Respiratory muscle failure is the danger (myasthenic crisis).
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Reflexes and sensation are preserved.** Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decrement at 2–3 Hz that recovers after brief exercise; antibody titres and single-fibre EMG help confirm. A neurologist must make the diagnosis for IVIg access.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Symptomatic treatment is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, mainly pyridostigmine,** but fewer than 20% of people with generalised MG stay stable long term on symptomatic treatment alone.
claims.source_text: For symptomatic therapy of MG, acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (AChE-I), primarily pyridostigmine, should be used. … However, only a small proportion of patients (<20%) with gMG are clinically stable in the long term with purely symptomatic therapy.
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Choose disease-modifying treatment by age, thymus pathology, antibody type and disease activity.** For mild to moderate generalised MG with AChR or LRP4 antibodies, or seronegative disease, start oral corticosteroids and/or azathioprine (with or without thymectomy); mycophenolate, ciclosporin, tacrolimus or methotrexate are second choice when azathioprine fails, is not tolerated or is contraindicated. Keep steroids to the shortest period at a dose matched to severity.
claims.source_text: Therapy must be based on age, thymic pathology, antibody status (AChR-Ab-, MuSK-Ab-, LRP4-Ab-positive as well as seronegative MG), and disease activity. … For AChR-Ab-positive, LRP4-Ab-positive, and seronegative gMG/jMG of mild/moderate activity, GKS and/or azathioprine (AZA; ± thymectomy) should be used as the first-choice therapy for disease course modification in addition to symptomatic therapy. … As an alternative to AZA, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), ciclosporin A (CSA), tacrolimus, or methotrexate (MTX) may be considered for second-choice treatment of gMG (to be used if AZA proves ineffective, is not tolerated, or is contraindicated). … Oral glucocorticosteroids (GKS) should be used to treat mild/moderate to (highly) active gMG/juvenile MG (jMG) and ocular MG (oMG) as basic immunotherapeutics at doses appropriate to disease severity over the shortest possible period of time, taking into account comorbidities, contraindications, and side effects.
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Azathioprine takes several months to work.** Start with 25–50 mg daily in the first week and increase over 3–4 weeks with regular blood tests, or after a 3-day trial of 50 mg daily move straight to 2–3 mg/kg daily; aim for a lymphocyte count of 600–1000/μl. Avoid giving it for more than 10 years because of malignancy risk.
claims.source_text: Due to the slow onset of action, therapeutic success with monotherapy is not to be expected before several months have elapsed. The therapy should be started with 25-50 mg daily in the first week and then gradually increased over 3-4 weeks under regular laboratory control. Alternatively, after a trial dose (of e.g. 50 mg daily for 3 days), a target dose of 2-3 mg/kg bw daily can be started more rapidly. An absolute lymphocyte count of 600-1000/μl is targeted during therapy. … so therapy with AZA over more than 10 years should generally be avoided
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Highly active or refractory generalised MG:** with AChR antibodies, add a complement inhibitor (eculizumab, ravulizumab) or an FcRn modulator (efgartigimod), with or without thymectomy; rituximab may be first choice with AChR or LRP4 antibodies or seronegative disease. IVIG and plasma exchange or immunoadsorption are second choice.
claims.source_text: Symptomatic therapy of (highly) active MG, including 'refractory to therapy', should be supplemented by the following disease-modifying therapies: In AChR-Ab-positive status, complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab) or FcRn modulators (efgartigimod) ± thymectomy should be selected. In AChR-Ab-positive, LRP4-Ab-positive, or seronegative status, CD20 antibody depletion (rituximab) ± thymectomy may be considered as first-choice therapy for disease course modification. Second-choice treatments are IVIG and plasmapheresis (common abbreviations: PLEX and PE; PE will be used hereafter)/immunoadsorption (IA).
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Eculizumab and other complement inhibitors raise the risk of meningococcal infection 1000- to 2000-fold.** Before starting, vaccinate against meningococcal serogroups A, C, W135, Y and B; give eculizumab at least 2 weeks after vaccination, or add antibiotic cover (rifampicin 600 mg every 12 h, or ceftriaxone 2 g daily; avoid quinolones, which can worsen MG). Patients carry a card and take an antibiotic and seek care at once if symptoms appear; follow up for at least 3 months after stopping.
claims.source_text: Prior to therapy with complement inhibitors, vaccination against meningococcal serogroups A, C, Y, W135 (1 × Menveo®), and B (2 × Bexsero® 4 weeks apart) must be performed. … Eculizumab is administered as an intravenous infusion started at least 2 weeks after meningococcal vaccination. If vaccine efficacy cannot be waited for or vaccine success cannot be assumed due to immunotherapy, prophylactic antibiotic therapy should be started in addition to vaccination. … Since quinolones can worsen MG, the following may be considered: rifampicin 600 mg p.o. every 12 h, taking into account interactions, or alternatively ceftriaxone 2 g i.v. every 24 h in case of intolerance. … Eculizumab is associated with a 1000- to 2000-fold increased risk of meningococcal infection due to its mechanism of action. Therefore, in addition to vaccination, patients should carry an eculizumab patient card and immediately contact their treating physician or an emergency department and take an antibiotic (such as 600 mg rifampicin p.o., ciprofloxacin p.o.) if symptoms of meningococcal infection occur. … Follow-up for at least 3 months should also be performed after completion of treatment.
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Eculizumab dose:** 900 mg IV weekly for the first four doses, then 1200 mg every 2 weeks from week 5. Treat as a response a fall in MG-ADL of at least three points and in QMG of at least 2.
claims.source_text: The first four administrations of eculizumab are at a dose of 900 mg once weekly. This is followed by administration of 1200 mg of eculizumab every 2 weeks starting at week 5. … Therapy success can be assumed if the MG-ADL score is reduced by at least three points and the QMG by ⩾2 points.
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Ravulizumab** is a longer-acting C5 inhibitor given every 8 weeks: weight-banded IV doses on day 1 and day 15 of 2400, 2700 or 3000 mg (for 40–60, 60–100 and over 100 kg), then 3000, 3300 or 3600 mg every 8 weeks, with the same meningococcal precautions.
claims.source_text: A further development of eculizumab is the complement factor 5 inhibitor ravulizumab, in which the infusion frequency of maintenance therapy is 8 weeks instead of two. … Infusion therapy is body weight-adapted (40-60 kg, 60-100 kg, >100 kg) on day 1 as well as day 15 at doses of 2400, 2700, or 3000 mg and every 8 weeks thereafter at doses of 3000, 3300, or 3600 mg. Safety precautions related to meningococcal vaccination and therapy, if necessary, are the same as those for eculizumab.
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **MuSK-antibody MG behaves differently:** its IgG4 antibodies do not bind complement, so C5 inhibitors have no target; pyridostigmine often works poorly or is poorly tolerated; thymectomy is not indicated; and rituximab should be considered early as a first-choice option.
claims.source_text: It is predominantly mediated by auto-Ab of the non-complement-binding IgG4 subclass, so C5-blocking drugs (e.g. eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan) have no target here. … Patients with MuSK-Ab-positive MG may respond poorly to AChE-I and more often tolerate it poorly. … Case series suggest that B-cell-depleting treatment with rituximab is effective, particularly in MuSK myasthenia, and should therefore be considered early as a first-choice treatment option as well. … Thymectomy is therefore not indicated for patients with MuSK myasthenia according to current data, nor is treatment with complement inhibitors.
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Look for thymoma in everyone with chest CT or MRI,** and remove a suspected thymoma as completely as possible. Without thymoma, thymectomy is advised for AChR-antibody-positive generalised MG aged 18–65, as early as possible: within 2 years and no later than 5 years from diagnosis.
claims.source_text: Every MG patient should be evaluated for the presence of a thymoma using thoracic computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging. If a thymoma is suspected, the thymus including thymoma should be surgically removed as completely as possible. … In patients with AChR-Ab-positive gMG aged 18-65 years, thymectomy (transsternal or minimally invasive) should be performed as early as possible within 2 years and no later than 5 years after confirmed diagnosis.
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Impending or established crisis: admit quickly to an intensive or monitored unit experienced in neuromuscular disease** and treat with IVIG or plasma exchange/immunoadsorption. These are equivalent; choose by comorbidity (plasma exchange is contraindicated in sepsis; IVIG in hypercoagulability, renal failure or immunoglobulin hypersensitivity) and local availability.
claims.source_text: In the event of an impending and manifest myasthenic crisis, rapid admission and treatment should be provided in a surveillance or intensive care unit with experience in neuromuscular diseases. IVIG or PE/IA should be selected as treatment in this situation. … Therefore, the decision for PE versus IVIG treatment will depend on individual patient factors such as concomitant diseases, in addition to local availability. For example, PE is contraindicated in sepsis and IVIG in hypercoagulability, renal failure, or existing hypersensitivity to Ig.
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **IVIg is funded for three MG situations, with clear evidence of benefit (Category 1):** myasthenic crisis and pre-operative or pre-thymectomy preparation (each as an alternative to plasma exchange), and maintenance of moderate to severe MG after other treatments have failed or were not tolerated.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IVIg and plasma exchange work about equally.** IVIg is simpler to give and plasma exchange is not offered everywhere; weigh line insertion, sepsis and haemodynamic risks of plasma exchange against the inflammatory and thrombotic risks of IVIg.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **In MuSK-antibody MG, plasma exchange is reported to work better than IVIg.**
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IVIg does not bring remission or change the course of MG,** so treat it as a bridge while symptomatic drugs such as pyridostigmine are used and definitive immunotherapy takes effect.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pure ocular MG is excluded,** and IVIg was generally ineffective for diplopia in the main trial.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Maintenance IVIg is not steroid-sparing,** in either the placebo-controlled trial or observational data.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Crisis:** respiratory insufficiency needing intubation and ventilation, or impending crisis (persistent trouble speaking, chewing or swallowing, or breathlessness on minimal exertion), plus severe disability with an MG Composite (MGC) score of 4 or more.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Before surgery or thymectomy:** an operation is planned and the patient has advanced disease, bulbar symptoms or respiratory involvement. Without those features, preparation is generally unnecessary.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Maintenance:** moderate to severe MG (MGC of 4 or more), at least two other treatments ineffective, contraindicated, unavailable or not tolerated, and the patient is not on a PBS-funded C5 inhibitor or FcRn inhibitor.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Crisis or pre-surgery: 1–2 g/kg split over 2 to 5 doses,** using the lowest dose that achieves the clinical goal.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **1 g/kg is as effective as 2 g/kg,** so make 1 g/kg the usual dose for worsening MG and keep 2 g/kg for crisis, impending crisis or especially severe disease.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Maintenance: after an induction dose, give 0.4–1 g/kg every 4–6 weeks,** titrated to response, and no more than 1 g/kg in any 4 weeks (smaller, more frequent doses are allowed).
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The German guideline doses differ slightly:** short-term IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for five days, or 1 g/kg daily for 2 days (a total of 1 g/kg may be enough); maintenance, used only in individual cases, a pulse and then 0.4 g/kg every 4–8 weeks or more if needed.
claims.source_text: Short-term treatment: IVIG should be administered at 0.4 g/kg bw for five consecutive days, alternatively 1 g/kg bw for 2 days. In individual cases, a lower total dose of 1 g/kg bw may be sufficient. … Based on expert knowledge, IVIG can be used for maintenance therapy over time in individual cases (initially 5 g/kg × 0.4 g/kg bw as a pulse, then 1 g/kg × 0.4 g/kg bw every 4-8 weeks or higher doses if clinically necessary)
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Give maintenance IVIg a 4-month trial (the induction dose and then 3 maintenance cycles);** stop if there is no benefit. A neurologist reviews within 4 months and yearly after that, and continuation needs documented effectiveness.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Measure response with the MG Composite:** at first review the score should have fallen by at least 3 points from qualifying (or a severe patient shows benefit after each infusion that wears off by cycle end), with at least two other treatments running concurrently where possible. Stable patients should have a planned weaning trial to detect remission.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The MGC is the practical clinical scale:** a 3-point or greater improvement is clinically meaningful. The longer Quantitative MG score, where above 11 predicts response to IVIg or plasma exchange, is mainly a research tool.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **LEMS is a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder,** first linked to lung cancer but also seen without a tumour. Look for proximal weakness that strengthens after exercise, mild eye signs, reduced reflexes and autonomic features (dry mouth, constipation, erectile failure). Confirm with voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies, electrophysiology or both.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **First-line LEMS treatment is 3,4-DAP (amifampridine) with pyridostigmine; IVIg is second line** and gives temporary benefit. In paraneoplastic LEMS, treating the cancer often helps, and immunosuppression (unlike IVIg) is generally avoided.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IVIg in LEMS qualifies when disease is severe** (MRC sum score 58 or lower, or major autonomic involvement) and other therapies have failed or fallen short. Dose: induction 2 g/kg over 2 to 5 doses, then 0.4–1 g/kg every 2–6 weeks.
claims.locator: National Blood Authority (NBA), Australia, 'Criteria for the Clinical Use of Immunoglobulin in Australia: Myasthenia gravis (MG), version 3.2, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), version 3.0', MG v3.2 published 22 May 2026; LEMS v3.0 published 20 October 2018, https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2765 (MG) and https://www.criteria.blood.gov.au/MedicalCondition/View/2563 (LEMS), retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **LEMS immunotherapy (international guideline):** corticosteroids at a severity-matched dose for as short a time as possible, azathioprine to spare steroids (alternatives mycophenolate, ciclosporin, tacrolimus or rituximab), and avoid methotrexate, especially in paraneoplastic LEMS. Use IVIG, or plasma exchange if needed, for crisis-like deterioration.
claims.source_text: GKS should be used for the treatment of LEMS as a basic immunotherapeutic agent at a dosage appropriate to the severity of the disease for as short a period as possible, taking into account comorbidities, contraindications, and side effects. AZA should be used for steroid-sparing therapy. As an alternative to AZA, the use of MMF, CSA, tacrolimus, or rituximab may be considered. MTX should be avoided, especially in pLEMS. IVIG or, if necessary, plasmapheresis should be used to treat a crisis-like deterioration.
claims.locator: German Neurological Society (DGN) guideline panel (Wiendl H, Abicht A, Chan A, et al.), Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders 16:17562864231213240, doi 10.1177/17562864231213240, 'Guideline for the management of myasthenic syndromes', published 26 December 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10752078/, retrieved 2026-09-24
